activities.text: Find a bug in a program or a spreadsheet.
Explain a hard topic to a friend so that they understand it.
Look after someone who has an injury.
Build something physical: a model, a piece of furniture, an electronic circuit.
Analyse data and find a pattern in it.
Talk to someone with a problem and help them find a way out.
Translate a text or a conversation so that nothing gets lost.
Plan a trip or an event and take care of the details.
Do an experiment in a lab and write down the results.
Write a text that moves or convinces someone.
Train regularly and track your progress.
Lead a training session or a warm-up for younger kids.
Take a device apart to understand how it works.
Convince a group of your idea.
Organise notes, files or photos so that everything is easy to find.
Find out how the human body or brain works.
Help someone from another country sort something out at an office or at the doctor's.
Write a simple program that saves someone time.
Work outside, in the field, in any weather.
Follow world news and understand why things happen.
Draw how something could look: a room, a poster or an object.
Sell something or negotiate a good price.
Film and edit a short video, or take photos that tell a story.
Design a game level or an app screen and check that nobody gets lost in it.
Play, sing or act in front of an audience.
Look after animals or plants, every day and properly.
Find a loophole in the rules or stand up for someone's cause.
Discover the history of an old place, building or object.
Cook something for others and work out what suits each person.
Do a survey and find out what people really think.
Solve a maths problem that nobody in the class can do.
Swim, sail or dive and find out what lives in the water.
Follow planes or rockets and understand how it all flies.
Discover new countries, people and food when you travel.
Go round museums and tell which period a painting or a building is from.
Read a contract or a set of rules and find what is wrong with it.
Draw a plan of a house or a housing estate and check that everything fits.
Design and 3D print a part that really works.
Run a class or a game for a group of younger children.
Check how an office or a school deals with something, and think of a simpler way.
Talk to people from different backgrounds and understand where inequality comes from.
Understand why something works in nature, from atoms to stars, until it all fits together.
Practise every day on an instrument, your voice or movement, so you can perform on stage.
Search an archive for old documents and check what really happened back then.
Help someone in a hard situation find the office or organisation that can help them.
Read the ingredients on products in a shop and plan a healthy menu for a whole week.
Help with animals at a shelter, in a stable or at a vet's.
Read maps and find out why a city grows here and not somewhere else.
Lead a group on a mountain trail or organise a camp in tents.

situations.text: Your group has to hand in a project tomorrow. The results do not add up, and one person is stressed and wants to give up. What do you do first?

answers.text: I sit down with the data and look for the mistake.
I talk to that person and share out the tasks again.
I suggest a different way of solving the whole problem.
I write to the teacher and ask for a later deadline.

situations.text: You have a free week and some money for a project of your own. What do you choose?

answers.text: A course or a book about something I finally want to understand.
I build or fix something with my own hands.
I organise a trip or an event for my friends.
I write, record or translate something of my own.
I volunteer where extra hands are needed.

situations.text: A friend twists their ankle at training. What do you do first?

answers.text: I look at the leg, raise it and put something cold on it.
I calm them down and stay with them.
I call for help and arrange how they get home.
I check what you should do for a sprain and tell the others.

situations.text: Your class is doing a joint project about your city. Which role do you take?

answers.text: Numbers, the survey and the charts.
Texts and the story.
Talking to the people who live there.
The plan, the deadlines and making sure it all comes together.
The technical side: photos, map, editing.

situations.text: There is a debate at school: should phones be banned during breaks? Which role do you take?

answers.text: I collect data and studies, so that the arguments have something to stand on.
I step forward and convince the room.
I listen to both sides and look for a solution that everyone accepts.
I make a poster or a short film that shows the problem.

situations.text: Your class has 3000 zloty for a trip, and you have to organise it. Where do you start?

answers.text: I work out the costs and compare offers in a table.
I ask everyone what they want and look for a compromise.
I call the transport company and negotiate a better price.
I check the route, the equipment and what could go wrong on the way.

situations.text: You get a week and a ticket to anywhere. Where do you go?

answers.text: To the sea: sailing, diving and finding out what lives under the water.
To a city full of museums, old churches and castles.
By plane as far as possible, to meet people and a different culture.
To the mountains, with a map and a tent, far from people.

situations.text: You lead a meeting of a club that wants to build a sports pitch next to the school. What do you take on?

answers.text: I check the rules and the permits we need.
I draw a plan of the pitch and work out how much material we need.
I look for machines and people to build it and make sure everything works.
I gather younger students to help and explain what they have to do.

situations.text: Your school is celebrating its 100th anniversary with an open day. What do you prepare?

answers.text: A survey of former students: what the school gave them and what they would change.
A show of physics and chemistry experiments, explaining what is happening.
A concert or a short scene to open the day, on stage in front of everyone.
An exhibition of old photos and documents from the school archive.

situations.text: Your class goes to a village near Kraków for a week. What do you want to be responsible for?

answers.text: The food: what we cook so that it is healthy and everyone likes it.
Helping on the farm with the horses, cows and hens.
The map of the area and the routes for the trips.
The games, the campfire and the evening programme for the whole group.

certainty.label: I know what I want to study
I have an idea, but I am not sure

studyLength.label: I want to start working soon (up to 3 years)
I do not mind long studies

doubts.label: I do not know what I like
doubts.card: That is normal. Look at what your answers already show: the strengths at the top of your results are yours, not made up.

doubts.label: I am afraid I will choose wrong
doubts.card: Your first choice is not a life sentence. You can change programme, and skills carry over between fields.

doubts.label: I am not good enough at one of the subjects
doubts.card: For every option you can see what it really needs and what you can do if something is missing. Not having an extended-level exam is something you can sort out, not a closed door.

doubts.label: Other people know what they want
doubts.card: Other people are often less sure than they look. What counts is the next step, not the whole plan.

doubts.label: I do not know if I can cope at university
doubts.card: The first year is mostly a new rhythm: more studying on your own and less checking up on you. Study groups, office hours with lecturers and student support offices (every big university has one) all help.

reflection.text: When did you last lose track of time? What were you doing?
What do you definitely not want to be doing in 10 years?
ideas: sitting at a desk all day
doing the same thing all the time

reflection.text: What do other people praise you for, even if it feels easy to you?

privateOk.label: Yes, if it is worth it
